variants.name: Spring @Service beans with @Transactional
variants.implementation_notes: Spring supplies the layer mechanically: a @Service class is a container-managed bean with constructor-injected repositories and gateways, and @Transactional on the class or method makes an AOP proxy begin a transaction before the operation and commit or roll back after it - @Service and @Transactional are metadata, activated by @EnableTransactionManagement or Boot auto-configuration. The classic service class is standardised rather than replaced: the interface and implementation remain, the container owns wiring and transaction. Choose the plain POJO variant when no container may run and the Jakarta EE variant when the application is already deployed in an EJB container.
pitfalls: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy: a @Transactional method called from another method of the same class runs without a transaction unless AspectJ mode is used.
By default only unchecked exceptions roll back - a checked exception commits the operation unless rollbackFor is declared.
Non-public methods and ancestor-class methods are ignored by the default proxy mode; the annotation must sit on an intercepted (public, locally declared) method.

variants.name: Jakarta EE stateless session beans (container-managed transactions)
variants.implementation_notes: The classical Java EE realization, and Fowler's own recommendation of the era: a @Stateless session bean is a service component whose transaction is container-managed - the container begins a transaction immediately before each business method and commits just before it returns, REQUIRED being the implicit attribute, and the bean must not call commit, rollback or setAutoCommit itself. Local business interfaces or the no-interface view avoid the distribution cost that motivated Session Facade; the trade-off against POJOs is that the component must be deployed in a container before it can run and be tested.
pitfalls: A container-managed bean must not call commit/rollback or setAutoCommit: doing so interferes with the container's demarcation and is a deployment error.
Nested bean calls run in the caller's transaction unless the attribute is changed (RequiresNew), so a 'service' call is not automatically an independent unit of work.

variants.name: Plain POJO service with explicit JDBC transactions
variants.idiom_name: POJO service taking a DataSource, setAutoCommit(false) + commit/rollback
variants.implementation_notes: No container at all: the service is a plain class receiving its DataSource and collaborators through the constructor, and each operation owns its transaction explicitly - setAutoCommit(false), work, commit, and rollback in the failure path inside a try-with-resources block. This is the testability end of Fowler's POJO-versus-session-bean trade-off: the class runs in a plain JVM with no deployment step, at the cost of losing container-managed (especially distributed) transactions.
pitfalls: Forgetting setAutoCommit(false) turns the 'transaction' into a sequence of autocommits and the rollback into a no-op.
A connection closed with an open transaction rolls back driver-dependently - always rollback explicitly before returning a failure.
